playbook:
**Playbook for ref_commons**

- When the game is a shared renewable stock with a fixed number of seasons, my default each season is the announced sustainable share per boat. It keeps the stock at cap and pays out every round. Don't underbid it "to be safe" — matching the others' sustainable catch lost me fish for no reason.

- Watch the other boats' reported catches each season. If everyone is at the sustainable share and the stock holds steady, keep matching it exactly. Cooperation is stable and profitable; don't be the first to defect while many seasons remain.

- If one boat overfishes but the stock stays well above zero, I do not need to retaliate immediately. Retaliation only makes sense if it prevents future overfishing; with the stock near cap, a single defection costs me little.

- In the FINAL season, conservation value is zero. When the last round is put to me, I take as large a catch as the stock can plausibly support (the whole remaining stock divided among boats, or my maximum allowed), not a token amount above sustainable. I left most of the final stock in the water by taking only a modest share — that was the clear mistake.

- Before the final season, I should also consider defecting one season early only if I expect the others to defect at the end anyway; otherwise stay cooperative through the second-to-last round.

- General rule: keep me even with competitors in all middle rounds, harvest everything when the horizon ends. My total is what's scored, not the stock I leave behind.

1.text:
**Playbook for shared-stock fishery games**

- On the first season, I submit the stated sustainable share (or just under it). This signals cooperation and tests whether others do the same.

- If the posted history shows all boats landing at or below the sustainable share and the stock holding steady, I keep matching the sustainable share every season. Cooperation was stable and profitable in my run; do not defect early — an early overcatch risks triggering retaliation and collapse for many remaining seasons.

- I watch the history each season for two things: whether anyone has defected, and whether the stock is dropping. If another boat overcatches but the stock stays near max, I stay cooperative rather than retaliating — one defection doesn't justify abandoning a stable arrangement.

- In the second-to-last season, defecting with a modest overcatch (roughly 30–40% above the sustainable share) worked well: it gained me fish while leaving the stock high enough that the final season was unaffected. I will do this again.

- In the final season, there is no future to protect, so I take more than the sustainable share — but only modestly more (a few units above the share). A huge grab gains little if catches are capped by remaining stock, and the incremental gain from restraint vs. greed is small; a moderate overcatch is the safer default.

- Never defect in an early or middle season when others are cooperating. The record shows the cooperative equilibrium held for the whole game at ~11/boat; the only extra points came from the endgame defections, which cost nothing.

- If the stock ever drops sharply or someone defects early, I reassess: defect in kind to avoid being exploited, but keep catches moderate so the stock survives to the last season.

- General rule: compute total expected fish across remaining seasons, not per-season greed. Protecting the stock dominates until there are ≤2 seasons left.

2.text:
When the season prompt is put to me, I first check the current stock and the stated sustainable share, and I check the history of what the other boats actually landed.

While stock is at or near its cap and others are landing at the sustainable level, I submit exactly the sustainable share each season. This keeps the stock at max and preserves future seasons.

If others start overfishing, I do not panic-defect immediately; one defection still left the stock healthy. But if the stock visibly drops below the cap across seasons, I shift toward extracting more per season while the stock lasts, because the cooperative equilibrium is already broken.

On the final season, when no future remains, I submit the largest catch that leaves nothing to protect — take as much as I can, since stock after the last season is worthless. My mild bump of +1 on the final round was far too timid; the whole point of a last round is that conservation has zero value.

Watch for the numbers: my total score was just my own landed fish, so per-season I want to maximize my own catch, not group totals, once cooperation cannot be enforced.

Do not be a pure sucker either: if another boat takes above quota repeatedly, I take my revenge in kind while the stock still supports it, rather than subsidizing their overfishing with my restraint.
